title: Early warning of critical transitions: Distinguishing supercritical and subcritical bifurcations from noisy observations
authors: Paul A. Sanders, Christian Kuehn, Bastian Hilder, Robbin Bastiaansen
abstract: Early-warning methods can indicate that a system is approaching a loss of stability, but they do not usually reveal whether the approaching bifurcation is supercritical or subcritical. We investigate whether this distinction can be made from noisy pre-transition observations. For this investigation, we extend a regression-based stability method by including the leading cubic nonlinear term, whose sign is used to predict the bifurcation type. We test the method on a stochastic pitchfork model and a spatial stochastic Swift-Hohenberg equation. In both models, classification improves with longer observation horizons, closer proximity to the bifurcation, stronger noise, and larger nonlinear effects. However, these conditions are also linked to a higher risk of noise-induced tipping in the subcritical case. The useful early-warning window is therefore determined by a balance between obtaining enough information to identify the bifurcation type and doing so before noise-induced tipping becomes too likely. In spatially extended systems, we find that observing the full spatial field allows classification over shorter observation horizons, and performance improves when a broader range of spatial modes contributes to the observed dynamics. Altogether, we identify the conditions under which the method can reliably distinguish between supercritical and subcritical bifurcations.
summary: This work develops a method to classify whether a system approaches a bifurcation in a supercritical or subcritical manner using noisy time-series data. By estimating the sign of the cubic nonlinear term from the dynamics, the authors show that this distinction is possible, provided the observation window is carefully chosen to balance information gathering against noise-induced tipping risks.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of distinguishing between supercritical and subcritical bifurcations from noisy, pre-transition observations, as standard early-warning methods only signal instability onset.
main_result: The distinction can be reliably made by estimating the sign of the leading cubic nonlinear term ($s$) from the dynamics, although this method requires balancing information gain against the increased risk of noise-induced tipping in the subcritical case.
method: The authors extend regression-based stability methods by incorporating the leading cubic nonlinear term into the normal form of the dynamics, analyzing both non-spatial and spatially extended systems.
model_or_system: The investigation uses the stochastic pitchfork model ($ rac{du}{dt} = \mu u + s u^3$) and the stochastic Swift-Hohenberg equation as test cases for pattern-forming systems near an instability.
key_observables: Estimated cubic coefficient ($\hat{s}$), linear stability parameter ($\hat{\mu}$), and the mean first passage time ($T(q)$) for exit time analysis.
important_parameters: Observation horizon ($	au_{\max}$), proximity to bifurcation ($\mu$), noise strength ($\sigma$), and the spatial wave number ($k^*$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the local dynamics can be accurately approximated by a minimal normal form containing linear and cubic nonlinear terms, and that the regression fits the deterministic drift while treating noise as a residual.
figures_summary: Figures show schematic comparisons of noisy trajectories, distributions of estimated coefficients ($\hat{s}$) for varying observation times, and how the Area Under the Curve (AUC) for classification improves with longer observation horizons or larger spatial fields.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for bifurcation type classification. It then details the regression-based method for both non-spatial (pitchfork) and spatially extended (Swift-Hohenberg) systems. Finally, it analyzes the performance dependence on observation time, noise, and spatial field size.
why_interesting: The techniques developed for analyzing critical slowing down and bifurcation type identification in noisy, non-equilibrium systems are highly relevant to understanding phase transitions and pattern formation in complex physical systems.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Mean first passage time for the subcritical reduced pitchfork model in Equa- tion (3.3). Starting from the stable equilibrium q = 0, the first passage time measures the average time required for a trajectory to reach either unstable threshold q = ±√−µ and leave the local stable region. The solid curve shows the mean first passage time obtained by numerically solving the backward boundary-value problem derived in Appendix A. The dashed curve shows the Eyring–Kramers approximation [26, 27], multiplied by an empirical factor C = 0.6 to improve the comparison over the finite parameter range shown.

Figure 3: Area under the ROC curve (AUC) as a function of parameter µ for the different observation horizons τmax. An AUC value of 0.5 indicates the classification method is as good as flipping a coin; an AUC value of 1 indicates potential for a perfect classification. µ indicates closeness to the bifurcation point located at µ = 0. A value of µ is shown only if at least 10% of the subcritical realizations remain within the local regime for the full observation horizon (Section 3.2); curves for longer horizons therefore end farther from the bifurcation. Some corresponding ROC-curves are shown in Figure 4.

Figure 4: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves for the stochastic pitchfork model in Equation (3.3) at observation horizons τmax = 10 (left) and τmax = 100 (right). Each curve corresponds to a different value of µ and is constructed from the fitted values of ˆs. The horizontal axis gives the false-positive rate and the vertical axis the true-positive rate, with the subcritical case (s = 1) taken as the positive class. The diagonal line denotes chance-level discrimination (i.e. flipping a coin).

Figure 5: Representative fitted dispersion relations for the stochastic Swift–Hohenberg model at γ = 1 and observation horizon τmax = 10. Each panel corresponds to a fixed combination of µ and s. The black curve shows the theoretical dispersion relation, the blue curve the ensemble mean of the fitted relations, and the dashed curves the 5th and 95th percentiles. Blue points denote the fitted maxima (ˆk∗, ˆλ∗) of the individual realizations, while the yellow star denotes the theoretical maximum (k∗, λ∗) = (1, µ). The text box reports the number of available realizations and summary statistics for ∆k = ˆk∗−k∗and ∆λ = ˆλ∗−λ∗, following [21].

Figure 6 shows the AUC for bifurcation criticality classification as a function of the distance to the bifurcation, µ, and the observation horizon, τmax, at fixed γ = 1. For a fixed observation horizon, the AUC generally increases as µ approaches zero, showing that the nonlinear coefficient becomes easier to distinguish closer to the bifurcation. At the same time, for a fixed value of µ, longer observation horizons lead to higher AUC values. Hence, as in the stochastic pitchfork model, a longer observation time allows the bifurcation type to be predicted farther away from the bifurcation point.
